string.name: help_layers
string.translation_description: Help section: the visible layers of the sky map. Please do not change the markup

resources.string:
Layers

Sky Map organises what it shows into layers, each of which can be toggled on or off independently via the layer buttons on the left-hand side. Long press, or tap the Layers button near the bottom, to bring up toggles for more layers.


Current layers include:
• Stars: The brightest stars, with labels for notable ones
• Constellations: Constellation outlines and names
• Deep-sky objects: Galaxies, nebulae, star clusters, and other remarkable objects
• Solar system: The Sun, Moon, and planets, displayed as images
• Meteor showers: The radiant points of the annual meteor showers
• Celestial grid: The right-ascension / declination coordinate grid
• Ecliptic: The Sun\'s annual path through the sky, which the Moon and planets roughly follow
• Horizon: The horizon line and cardinal direction labels (N, S, E, W)
• Sky gradient: The daytime sky glow and twilight colouring near the horizon

The meteor shower radiants only show on the dates when the meteor showers are happening.

How big the planets are drawn

Tap the arrow beside Solar system in the Layers sheet to choose how the Sun, Moon and planets are sized:

• Glyphs (the default): big enough to see at any zoom, and sized by how big each body actually is rather than how big it looks from here — a model of the solar system rather than a view through a telescope. Saturn and its rings are the widest thing of all, then the Sun, then Jupiter, down to Pluto. The differences are squeezed to fit the screen: the Sun is really 586 times Pluto\'s width, not seven. The Moon is the exception, drawn the same size as the Sun, because that is how the two look from here.
• True scale: every body at its real size in the sky. The Sun and Moon are about half a degree across — roughly a pencil rubber held at arm\'s length — and the planets are specks until you zoom right in. Zoom all the way and Jupiter shows its belts, Saturn\'s rings separate from the planet, and an eclipse lines up exactly as it does in the sky.
• Steady: holds each body at a fixed size on the screen as you zoom, switching to the real size once you are zoomed in far enough for it to be the larger of the two.

The two modes tell you different things. Glyphs says Jupiter is a giant and Pluto is tiny. True scale says the Sun and Moon look almost exactly the same size from Earth — which is why a total solar eclipse works at all, and you can watch it happen.
Sky Map shows the geometric horizon — a perfectly flat, unobstructed view. Objects just above it may still be hidden by buildings, hills, or trees in practice.

string.name: help_info_cards
string.translation_description: Help section: the object info cards. Please do not change the markup

resources.string:
Info Cards

Tap a labelled celestial object on the Sky Map to bring up an info card — a panel with a photo and details about that object. Info cards are available for hundreds of objects including stars, planets, the Moon, notable deep-sky objects, and constellations.


Each card shows:

• A photograph or chart of the object
• A short description and a fun fact
• Scientific data such as distance, size, and object type

Tap the image inside the card to view it fullscreen. Dismiss the card by tapping outside it or pressing Back.

Not all objects have info cards, but we\'re adding more all the time.

string.name: help_search
string.translation_description: Help section: searching for objects in the sky. Please do not change the markup

resources.string:
Search

Tap the magnifier button (bottom) to search for anything in the sky.


You can search for:

• Stars — by name, e.g. "Sirius", "Betelgeuse", "Polaris"
• Planets — e.g. "Mars", "Saturn"
• Constellations — e.g. "Orion", "Cassiopeia"
• Deep-sky objects — e.g. "M31", "Andromeda Galaxy", "Pleiades"
• Coordinates — right ascension and declination, e.g. "5h 55m, 7° 24\'" (you can use an \'o\' for a degree symbol)

In Auto Mode: after selecting a result, Sky Map shows a targeting circle and a directional arrow. Follow the arrow by rotating your phone — the circle changes colour as the object comes into your field of view. Tap Cancel (or press Back) to exit search.

In Manual Mode: the map simply jumps to centre on the object.

You can search for objects that Sky Map doesn\'t show such as Europa, one of Jupiter\'s moons. In this case, search will lead you to the parent object (Jupiter).

string.name: help_time_travel
string.translation_description: Help section: the time travel feature. Please do not change the markup

resources.string:
Time Travel

Time Travel lets you see the sky at any moment from the year 1600 to 3000. Tap the clock button (bottom).


Pick a popular event (eclipses, meteor-shower peaks, the next full or new moon, planet conjunctions, the Apollo 11 landing, and more) from the event list, set your own moment with the Set date and Set time buttons, or tap "Start from now" if you simply want to go forwards or backwards from the current moment.

Once in Time Travel mode, the date is shown on screen and playback controls let you move through time:

• Tap ▶▶ (faster) or ◀◀ (slower) to step the playback speed forward or backward through time
• Tap ❚❚ to pause
• Tap Now to jump back to the present

Some things you can use it for:

• What can I see just after sunset tonight?
• When is the next good chance to spot Mercury?
• What did the sky look like the night I was born?

Accuracy decreases for dates far from the present, mainly due to the gravitational influence of Jupiter.
